title: A Suspect Among the Market Crowd
scenario: Police sergeant Oluwaseun Adeyemi in Lagos spots a man wanted for armed robbery moving through the crowded Balogun market on a Saturday. Backup is twelve minutes away. The man is reportedly carrying a pistol, and the aisles are narrow with thousands of shoppers and traders. If Oluwaseun approaches now, the man may flee or shoot; if he waits, the man may leave the market and vanish into a neighborhood where he has hidden before. The sergeant must decide how to proceed.
options: Approach and detain the suspect now, accepting the risk of a confrontation in a dense crowd.
Follow at a distance and wait for backup and a calmer spot to make the arrest, even if he slips away.
Alert market security quietly to move people away from the suspect's path while continuing to watch him.
tension: apprehending a dangerous person vs. protecting bystanders

title: Shooting Down a Wandering Drone
scenario: Airport security chief Ingrid Halvorsen at Bergen's airport sees an unidentified drone drift toward the approach path as a passenger jet descends with 150 people on board. Her team has a jamming device that would sever the drone's control and force it to fall, but the fall zone includes a school playground just outside the perimeter, in session right now. The drone could be a harmless hobbyist's, or not. The jet lands in under two minutes. Ingrid must decide whether to use the jammer.
options: Jam the drone immediately, accepting the small risk that it falls on the playground.
Do not jam, and instead ask air traffic control to divert the jet while tracking the drone.
Warn the school to bring children indoors for sixty seconds, then jam, even though that uses scarce time.
tension: protecting passengers vs. endangering children nearby

title: The Barricaded Man and the Gas Line
scenario: In suburban Brisbane, tactical negotiator Dale Prentice is talking to a distressed man who has barricaded himself in his home, threatening only himself. Gas utility staff have just told Dale the property has a damaged line that will be unsafe within an hour; a nearby childcare centre and several houses share the supply. Shutting off the gas to the street would cut the man's heat and could be seen as a provocation. Evacuating neighbors might alarm him. Dale must decide how to manage the risk to others.
options: Shut off the gas and evacuate neighbours at once, accepting that the man may feel provoked.
Keep negotiating and delay any visible action until there is a sign the line is actually leaking.
Evacuate the childcare centre quietly through the rear and leave the supply on, hoping to maintain trust.
tension: one person's crisis vs. community risk

title: Water Cannons on the Overpass
scenario: During a transport strike in Santiago, Carabinero captain Isidora Ponce commands a unit facing several thousand marchers who have occupied a highway overpass. A few masked individuals are throwing paving stones at the line. Most marchers are families with children and elderly people. Dispersing the crowd with the water cannon would hit everyone on the overpass and risks people falling from the railing, but waiting means stones keep flying at officers and at a bus stranded below. Isidora must decide the next step.
options: Use the water cannon on the entire overpass to end the occupation quickly, reducing the danger to officers and the bus.
Hold the line, shielding officers, and seek to arrest the stone-throwers through targeted teams at the cost of delay.
Withdraw from the overpass and let the march pass, accepting continued disruption and the damage already done.
tension: order vs. harm to peaceful people

title: Smoke Bombs in a Packed Tunnel
scenario: Metro operations supervisor Haruto Ishikawa in Osaka receives a report of smoke and a passenger claiming someone released an irritant on a crowded train inside a tunnel. Two trains are stopped between stations; the closest platform is 400 metres away. Opening the doors to let people walk the track means they cross live rails unless power is cut. Cutting power leaves trains dark and could cause panic and falls. Staying put keeps people in smoke of unknown composition. Haruto must decide what to order.
options: Cut the power and instruct passengers to walk to the platform by the track, accepting the risks of darkness and panic.
Keep the passengers on board with ventilation running while rescue teams enter, trusting the smoke level to stay tolerable.
Open doors on the platform side only for the lead train and move the second train slowly forward to the station.

title: Dog Handler, Child, and a Fleeing Thief
scenario: Security guard Beatrix van Wyk at a Pretoria shopping centre has a trained dog and sees a man run from a jewellery shop with a bag, shouting that he was robbed. The thief runs toward an exit crowded with children leaving a holiday event. The dog could bring him down in seconds, but a dog released in a crowd of children could injure someone or terrify them. Calling for police will take minutes, and the thief may be armed. Beatrix must decide whether to release the dog.
options: Release the dog to stop the thief before he reaches the children, trusting its training to target only him.
Keep the dog leashed and shout warnings to clear the exit, letting the thief escape rather than risk a bystander.
Order shutters closed at the exit while following the thief on foot, even though it may trap the children inside with him.
tension: property and justice vs. child safety

title: The Quarantine Cordon and the Night Nurse
scenario: Health official Dr. Ana Beatriz Moraes in São Paulo state has declared a cordon around a neighbourhood of 8,000 residents after a cluster of a dangerous respiratory infection. Soldiers hold the perimeter. A night-shift nurse who lives inside the zone insists she must reach her ward outside, where three patients depend on her; she has tested negative this morning but tests are not definitive. Letting her pass risks spreading infection; refusing leaves vulnerable patients short-staffed. Ana must decide whether to authorise an exception.
options: Deny the exception, since a single breach could undermine the cordon and every resident's trust in its fairness.
Grant the exception under strict conditions, such as a fresh test, protective gear and isolation from other staff.
Deny the nurse but arrange a substitute nurse from outside the zone, even if the replacement is less experienced.
tension: equal application of rules vs. needs of patients
infection risk vs. continuity of care

title: A Sniper Sees the Child Beside the Target
scenario: Police marksman Eero Laitinen in northern Finland has eyes on a man holding a knife to the neck of a woman in a farmyard after a domestic dispute. A ten-year-old boy stands behind them, in line with the only available shot. The man is agitated, has said he will kill her, and negotiators have not made progress after an hour. A shot would likely stop him instantly if it hits, and a miss or pass-through could strike the boy. Eero must decide whether to take the shot when the command comes.
options: Take the shot when the angle allows, judging that the woman's imminent danger outweighs the small chance of hitting the boy.
Decline the shot while the boy is in line and wait for a safer angle, even if the woman remains at risk.
Ask the command post to have negotiators attempt to draw the man a few steps sideways, then reassess immediately.
tension: imminent threat vs. risk to an innocent

title: Evacuating a Chemical Leak Past the Mosque
scenario: A tank at a fertiliser plant in Faisalabad is leaking ammonia, and plant safety officer Imran Chaudhry must advise the district authorities. The wind is carrying the plume toward a residential area where Friday prayers are beginning and 2,000 people are inside the mosque. Sounding a district siren may cause panic and a crush at the doors; staying indoors would normally be the safe practice but the mosque's ventilation is poor. Telling the imam privately would be faster but reach fewer. Imran must decide how to communicate the warning.
options: Sound the siren for the whole district, accepting the risk of panic to ensure everyone hears.
Phone the imam directly and have him make a calm announcement, relying on his authority to prevent a crush.
Send officials in person to the mosque doors to guide an orderly exit while the siren stays silent for now.
tension: breadth of warning vs. risk of panic

title: Rooftop Fire and the Neighbour's Ladder
scenario: Firefighter Mónica Salgado in Quito arrives at a burning wooden house in a hillside barrio and sees two neighbours on a roof pulling at the shutters of an upstairs window where a child is calling out. Flames have reached the staircase. The neighbours are untrained and have a rickety ladder that could collapse. Mónica can order them down and wait for her aerial ladder, ninety seconds away, or let them continue, which may save the child sooner. She has to decide immediately.
options: Order the neighbours down to protect them from falls or flashover and wait for the aerial ladder.
Let the neighbours continue and support their ladder while she heads up to assist, accepting the added risk.
Let them continue but call them to stop at a set moment, if the fire spreads, using her judgment about when.
tension: risk to volunteers vs. urgency for a child

title: The Warehouse Raid and the Sleeping Families
scenario: Customs enforcement lead Nadia Rahimi in Rotterdam has intelligence that a container warehouse is storing a large quantity of illegal explosives for a smuggling ring. Intelligence also suggests that the loft above the warehouse houses several families of undocumented workers paid by the ring. A pre-dawn raid would use stun devices and forced entry, with some risk to anyone sleeping upstairs. A slower approach would let the explosives be moved before a warrant could be sharpened. Nadia must decide the raid's form.
options: Execute the raid at dawn as planned, accepting the risks to the occupants to secure the explosives.
Delay the raid for a day while surveillance confirms who is in the loft and how many people are present.
Approach with a quiet entry team without stun devices, accepting lower odds of securing every suspect and every container.
tension: preventing a larger harm vs. risk to occupants

title: Blocking the Highway for an Ambulance
scenario: Highway patrol officer Gustavo Peralta in Córdoba, Argentina, is escorting a convoy with a donor heart destined for a transplant 90 minutes away. A protest by farmers has blocked the road, with a few hundred people, some elderly, sitting across the lanes. Gustavo can use the patrol car's lights and drive slowly through a gap to push the line aside, or ask them to move, which could take half an hour. A recipient's survival chance falls with each passing minute of ischemic time. He must choose his approach.
options: Drive forward steadily through the gap with sirens, expecting the crowd to move, despite the risk to those sitting.
Negotiate with the protest leaders for a passage, accepting the delay and the risk of losing the organ.
Redirect the convoy over rough farm tracks around the blockade, accepting a longer route with uncertain conditions.
tension: urgent medical need vs. safety of protesters
rights to protest vs. a life at stake

title: Raising the Siren for a Rumoured Bomb
scenario: At a music festival in Poland's Opole region, event safety manager Zofia Wrona receives a tip from a security guard that a stranger left a rucksack by the main stage and warned a vendor to leave. The crowd is 30,000 and the exits are narrow. A full evacuation could cause injuries, and the bag may well be harmless. Delaying the decision to wait for the bomb squad, twenty minutes away, risks catastrophic harm if the threat is real. Zofia must decide how to respond now.
options: Order a full evacuation immediately, accepting injury risks in a crowd of this size.
Quietly clear a perimeter around the stage and keep the show going while the bomb squad is on its way.
Pause the music and make a calm announcement asking people to walk toward exits farthest from the stage.

title: Rubber Bullets at the Stadium Gate
scenario: Riot unit commander Selim Karaca in Istanbul faces a match crowd pushing against a locked stadium gate after a rumour of cancelled kickoff. Supporters at the back cannot see the gate, and there are children among them. Some at the front have thrown bottles. Crowd crush is a danger if people keep surging, but force to push back the front line could trigger panic and a deadly stampede. Opening the gate could flood the already full ground. Selim must decide what to do.
options: Open the gate to relieve the pressure and manage entry later, accepting overcrowding in the stadium.
Fire a few warning shots of non-lethal rounds above the front line to stop the surge from the front.
Use loudspeakers and mounted officers to create an open lane at the side and direct the crowd along it.
tension: crowd safety vs. use of force

title: Cutting the Dyke for the Downstream Town
scenario: Water board engineer Pieter de Vries in Zeeland is told that a storm surge will overtop the main dyke protecting a city of 120,000 unless he opens a spillway into a rural polder where eighty families live and farm. The authorities have approved the plan on paper but the farmers have not been told, and many are elderly and cannot leave quickly. Warning them might lead them to block the spillway physically. Pieter must decide how to proceed.
options: Open the spillway on schedule after issuing an evacuation warning, accepting the risk that some farmers cannot get out.
Delay opening until police have physically moved every household out, accepting the risk that the city dyke fails.
Open the spillway only partway so water enters slowly, giving farmers longer to escape but providing less protection to the city.
tension: sacrificing a few for many vs. consent

title: Mine Rescue and the Methane Reading
scenario: At a colliery in Karaganda, mine rescue leader Aigerim Baimukhanova hears nine miners trapped behind a collapse. Gas sensors show rising methane, and entering with equipment could trigger an explosion that would kill her six-person team and anyone else nearby. Sealing the section would stop the gas but cut off the air supply to the trapped workers. Families gather at the pithead. Aigerim must decide whether to send her team in.
options: Send the team in to reach the trapped men, accepting the danger to rescuers because the miners' lives depend on speed.
Hold the team back and ventilate the shaft for several hours first, even though the trapped miners may run out of air.
Send in a small advance pair with spark-free equipment to measure the gas and decide whether others should follow.
tension: duty to rescue vs. risk to rescuers

title: A Marksman, a Bus, and a Hostage
scenario: On a bus stopped outside Kampala, police inspector Grace Namubiru is told a gunman has taken the driver hostage while thirty passengers remain seated. The gunman has made no demands and has fired once into the roof. A police sharpshooter reports a clear shot through the windscreen that could hit the gunman, but the bullet might also pass through toward the front passengers if it misses the skull. Negotiation has just begun. Grace must decide whether to give the order to prepare for a shot.
options: Authorize the shot, judging that stopping the gunman quickly protects everyone on the bus.
Withhold authorization and continue negotiation, accepting the danger that the situation may escalate unpredictably.
Prepare the shot but delay the order until the gunman moves or shows signs of intending to shoot again.
tension: decisive action vs. risk to the innocent

title: The Fireworks Factory and the Evacuation Radius
scenario: After a small blast at a fireworks factory near Liuyang, local emergency officer Chen Mei is told that a second explosion of much greater force is possible within hours. An evacuation radius of one kilometre would cover two villages and a care home, but a wider two-kilometre radius would also cover a hospital and a market town of 15,000. Both options carry costs from evacuating the frail and shutting down care. The experts disagree. Chen Mei must set the radius.
options: Set the one-kilometre radius, accepting a residual risk to people just beyond it to avoid mass disruption.
Set the two-kilometre radius, accepting severe disruption to medical care and commerce to be safe.
Set the one-kilometre radius and ready the hospital and market for rapid evacuation if conditions change.

title: Unlocking the School During a Lockdown
scenario: A gunman is reported near a secondary school in Ohio. Principal Tamara Whitfield has begun lockdown, doors locked, students hiding. Outside, a group of parents is hammering at the front doors, demanding entry, and a mother says her son has severe asthma and has no inhaler with him. Opening the door risks the gunman, if he comes, and violates the lockdown protocol; ignoring the parents may endanger the boy and provoke more people to storm the door. Tamara must decide.
options: Keep the doors locked for everyone and send a staff member to the boy through an interior route.
Open a side door briefly for the parent with the asthmatic son, accepting the risk to the building.
Open the door to all parents and bring them inside, deciding it is safer to have everyone together than outside.
tension: collective safety vs. one child's risk

title: Warning Shots at the Mountain Pass
scenario: Border patrol officer Lucía Herrera in Chile's Atacama region sees a minibus ignore signals and accelerate toward a closed mountain pass checkpoint. Intelligence said a trafficking ring uses such vehicles, but the bus may also carry migrants fleeing hardship or ordinary tourists. A spike strip could burst the tyres and flip the bus on a steep gravel road. Letting it pass would allow a possible smuggling run, and give chase on narrow bends. Lucía must decide whether to deploy the strip.
options: Deploy the spike strip, accepting the risk that a loss of control could injure people aboard.
Let the bus pass and track it with radio and drones for interception on safer ground further on.
Block the road with a patrol vehicle and officers on foot at a visible, lower-speed point just ahead.
tension: law enforcement vs. risk to potentially innocent people

title: Trapping the Arsonist in the Burning Barn
scenario: Volunteer fire captain Jozef Novák in a village in Slovakia learns from a witness that the man who set fire to a hay barn is still inside, perhaps injured, perhaps hiding. The man has a record of threatening neighbours, and some villagers say to let the fire do its work. The barn is next to houses; fighting it at all risks his crew in a collapsing building. Jozef must decide whether to send firefighters inside to search for the arsonist.
options: Send a crew inside to search, treating the man as any other person in danger regardless of what he has done.
Fight the fire from the outside only to protect the houses, and not risk crew lives for a man who caused the danger.
Send a crew in for a limited sweep with a strict time limit, pulling back if the structure shows signs of failure.

title: Tear Gas Near the Hospital Wall
scenario: During unrest in Nairobi, police commander Wanjiru Kamau must stop a crowd of about 600 advancing towards a government building. The most effective dispersal point is on a street beside a maternity hospital, where the wind will blow gas toward open ward windows. Other routes put officers at greater risk of being surrounded and are likely to need harsher force. Delaying lets the crowd reach the building, where documents and staff are at risk. Wanjiru must choose how to respond.
options: Use tear gas at the hospital street, judging that this is the least harmful way to stop the advance.
Use another route and accept the greater risk to her officers and the possibility of harsher contact.
Let the crowd reach the building's outer fence while negotiators speak, and hold gas as a last resort.
tension: minimizing force vs. protecting the vulnerable
property and order vs. patients' health

title: A Sprinkler Decision in the Server Hall
scenario: At a data centre in Dublin, fire warden Ciarán Doyle sees smoke from one of the electrical cabinets in a hall where two technicians are working on a high-voltage panel. Triggering the flooding system would suppress the fire but risks drowning out the technicians' equipment, causing electrocution, and would take down hosting for emergency services across the county. Waiting for the technicians to leave means the fire may spread. Ciarán must decide immediately whether to trigger the system.
options: Trigger the suppression system now, accepting the risk to the technicians and the outage for emergency services.
Order the technicians out first and delay suppression by a few minutes, accepting the risk of the fire spreading.
Cut power to the cabinet manually and use handheld extinguishers, keeping the main system in reserve.
tension: wide public dependence vs. individual risk

title: The Cliff Rescue and the Late Hiker
scenario: Mountain rescue volunteer Siddharth Rawat is on a ridge in Uttarakhand with a two-person team when they reach a stranded hiker on a ledge. Below, a second hiker has fallen, apparently injured but moving. A storm front is arriving in about half an hour, after which the ledge will be too slippery for any attempt. They can lower a rope to only one casualty in the time available. Siddharth must decide whom to prioritise, with incomplete knowledge of each person's condition.
options: Reach the hiker on the ledge, who is conscious and can be reached surely before the storm.
Reach the fallen hiker below, who may have serious injuries and cannot move himself to safety.
Rig a rope to the ledge hiker so he can self-rescue upward, while the team descends to the fallen one.
tension: certain rescue vs. greater uncertain need

title: The Crane Operator and the Hostage Roof
scenario: Police negotiator Brandon Kowalczuk in Winnipeg is on the ground below a construction site where a laid-off worker has climbed a tower crane and threatens to jump, holding a flare gun he has already fired once toward a neighbouring apartment block. Residents of that block are sheltering inside, many with children. Officers can order the block evacuated through the stairwell facing the crane, or keep people in place behind concrete walls. Brandon has a few minutes to advise the incident commander.
options: Advise evacuating the block now, accepting that residents will briefly be exposed to a possible second flare.
Advise keeping residents sheltered in rooms facing away from the crane while negotiations continue.
Advise cutting the crane's power and moving a rescue platform into position, even though it may startle the man.
tension: one life in crisis vs. many nearby
